implementation_notes: The collaborator's members are replaced by jest.fn() functions configured in the test: mockReturnValue(v) for a fixed answer, mockImplementation(fn) when the answer depends on the arguments, mockResolvedValue/mockRejectedValue for promises and the ...Once variants for a single call, with mock.calls and mock.results recording what happened for later assertions. The test runner itself provides the double, so no double class exists and the configuration sits next to the assertion; Jest documents mock functions as spies and records the arguments and results of every call (mock.calls, mock.results), so the same object is control point and observation point. Prefer it whenever the collaborator is an injected object or module whose methods can be replaced.
pitfalls: Configured implementations and recorded calls live on the mock, so mocks reused across tests must be reset (mockReset/mockClear) or the next test inherits them.
Unconfigured mock functions return undefined, so a test can pass while the SUT silently took a path that was never intended; configure explicit defaults for the happy path.
Module mocks (jest.mock) are hoisted above imports, so a double installed that way replaces the dependency for the whole file and hides the real wiring.

variants.name: Hand-written configurable object or class
variants.idiom_name: reusable class/object literal with settable response fields
variants.implementation_notes: A plain class or object literal implements the collaborator's method names and reads its canned answers from fields the test assigns, so the double works under any runner (node:test, Mocha, Jest) and needs no test-framework mocking API; throwing is how a failure is configured and an array of recorded calls is how the same object doubles as a spy. This is the framework-free route and the right one when the cooperation is small or when the double must also carry a little real logic such as an in-memory queue.
pitfalls: Because the double is not checked against the real collaborator, a renamed or misspelled method is only discovered when the SUT calls it.
An object literal reused across tests carries the previous test's configured fields; construct a fresh double in setup instead of mutating a shared one.
Returning the wrong type (undefined for an awaited call, a plain object where a promise is expected) makes the SUT fail in a way that looks like a production bug.
